motilli.copy: If you're backed up on a GLP-1 and eating less isn't helping, let me explain the gut slowdown nobody warned me about. Because once I understood it, everything changed.
Because I was dropping weight. Like, the shot was actually working. But I felt backed up every single day, that uncomfortable fullness that just wouldn't shift no matter what I ate or didn't eat.
And that's the bit that messed with my head. My jeans were getting looser but I was still picking outfits around how my stomach felt. And I didn't really know how to explain that to anyone.
So let me tell you what I was actually missing because I genuinely thought losing the weight would fix it.
I was just scrolling through a GLP-1 support group on Facebook looking for answers and a gastroenterologist had left a comment on someone's post and it stopped me mid-scroll.

He said GLP-1 meds can slow down how fast your stomach empties. Like your stomach normally contracts to push food through, and when that slows down everything just backs up. Food, waste, gas. That's where the backed-up bloated feeling is actually coming from. It wasn't a weight thing at all. It was the gut slowdown.

And I thought okay, so that's why the fiber wasn't doing anything. Because fiber helps with regularity and MiraLAX moves water into the stool. Neither one actually touches the stomach emptying speed. I had completely missed that.
So I went back and DM'd him. I just asked what actually helps with the slowdown.
He wrote back. He said to look for ingredients that support gastric motility specifically. Something that helps the gut wall contract and actually move things through.
So I went back to the group and posted the question. And this woman who'd been on Ozempic for about eight months replied.
She said she'd spent months researching this and found three specific ingredients that research showed actually addressed the gut slowdown directly. She walked me through each one.
First was apigenin, which comes from celery juice. It's been shown in research to activate the receptors in the gut wall that trigger those contractions. The ones that actually move food forward.
Second was chlorophyllin, a plant compound. It's been studied clinically to bind the gas-producing stuff in the gut before it gets a chance to build pressure.
Third was a soluble prebiotic fiber. But she was specific about it because the wrong type or too much can actually make the gas worse, not better.

But she said she'd spent months trying to put it together herself first. Celery juice powder on its own. Chlorophyll supplements. Different fiber products. She tried all of it. None of it moved the needle the same way. She said the ratios have to be right and you can't just piece them together and get the same effect.
And the thing was, she'd looked. She couldn't find a single company that had put all three together properly. Until she found one.
It was a gummy called Motilli.
You take two before bed with a full glass of water which I honestly preferred because I'd already had enough capsules to last me a lifetime.
And the first week, honestly, I saw no change. I nearly messaged her to say it wasn't working but I thought fine, I'll give it more time.

Then around week two I had dinner with my husband and I got through the whole meal without thinking about my stomach once. Like I wasn't sitting there quietly uncomfortable the entire time waiting for it to pass. That sounds like nothing but I hadn't had that in months.

By week three my mornings felt different. That heavy backed-up feeling when I woke up had started to ease. I wasn't laying there feeling like nothing had moved all night or rushing to the bathroom in a panic before I'd even had coffee.

And the real test was just whether I could eat a normal amount and feel fine after. Not fine after I'd walked around the block and waited for it to settle. Just fine. Around the five or six week mark that was actually happening.
So that was me two months ago. This is me now.

I get through dinner without planning to undo my jeans by dessert. That backed-up pressure that used to build from just a few bites has gone. I'm not mapping out my outfit in the morning around how uncomfortable I think I'm going to feel by lunchtime.

And I know the shot gets credit for the weight coming off. But the part that made me feel like myself again was getting rid of that constant uncomfortable feeling. Because you can be losing weight on a GLP-1 and still feel awful every single day. And nobody talks about that part. I'm sharing this because nobody told me either.

The only thing she mentioned, and I've found this too, is they only do batches when the full formula is ready. So I've started ordering a spare bottle halfway through mine just so I'm not sitting around waiting on the next one.

nuora.copy: So last year's rebound had me packing a second charity bag of clothes, bringing coverups tothe pool, and literally refusing family holiday picks because my doc told me the only way I'd shift the meno weight was with skinny shots until I proved him wrong. But the final straw for me was the horrors I had while on the shots my doc recommended. The nausea got so bad, I'd feel too dizzy to even safely do school pickup just for a few lousy pounds off the scale. All while my doc never even bothered to look at the new science because why would he? He didn't cry in the mornings at the stupid weight not shifting or feel embarrassed to go out in anything but stretchy joggers and a baggy t shirt. *

But in the next thirty seconds, I'm gonna tell you what I found that took me from being ashamed to be in my swimsuit among friends to actually buying even cuter ones. And it uses the same science that's helping thousands of other women quietly reclaim themselves again. So let me show you how.

So, of course, I didn't hear this from a doctor, but a five minute reply from a gut practitioner on a menopause health forum. She explained it like this.

If you take your tongue right now and run it across your teeth, unless you've just brushed them, you'll feel a thin slimy plaque layer. Well, the same thing happens in the gut, [obscured] to brush it away. But why does this gut plaque matter? Well, because estrogens helps the good bacterial plaque in the gut. But when it declines after menopause, this layer dies off, and the bad bacteria that would usually get brushed out by the good start to build up to form what gut researchers call biofilms. So it thickens over the years and starts to block absorption and inflame the gut. Vitamins can't get through, minerals can't get through, and the good stuff from food starts bouncing off. So before you know it, the body's raising the cortisol alarms in a panic. ‘And where does this cortisol go? Well, the place with four times four cortisol receptors than anywhere else in the body, the belly.
So my mind started racing. Like, was this why the pooch wouldn't budge? Why I felt so exhausted by pickup and puffy even in the mornings? How do I stop it?

She explained that a research team in Milan wanted to answer the same question. So they invested millions, flying in researchers from around the world to test everything they could against these biofilms.
Probiotics? Nope. Antibiotics? Nope. But then they found something that shocked even them.
You know the tingly mouth feeling from eating too much pineapple? Well, that's bromelain, eating the bacteria slime off your tongue, and this ‘same friendly enzyme breaks down biofilm [obscured] gut.

Before finding, when they slowly freeze dried the enzymes before packaging, it made them three times as effective at breaking the biofilms. I was thinking, well, that's great for the puffiness and bloat, but what about my pooch? But she explained, pairing it with some berberine is the missing key, and it's where most companies go wrong.
